challenges.name: es-modules-evaluation-quiz
challenges.title: Predict how Node evaluates your modules
challenges.description: Three small module graphs: in which order do the bodies run, what does an importer see after an exported variable changes, and what does top-level await really pause?

questions.explanation: Import declarations are hoisted: Node loads and links the whole graph before any module body runs, no matter where the import lines are written. Evaluation is depth-first and dependencies come first: c.js (first dependency of a.js), then a.js, then b.js, whose dependency c.js has already been evaluated and is not run again, and finally main.js. A module body runs once per process; every later import gets the same cached module.

A named export of a variable is a live binding: main.js reads the variable inside counter.js, so after inc() it sees 1. `export default count` exports the value of an expression, evaluated once when counter.js ran, so the default import stays 0. Imported bindings are read-only in the importing module: `count = 5` in main.js throws "TypeError: Assignment to constant variable."; only counter.js can change it, for example through inc(). And counter.js is evaluated once: every module that imports it shares the same count.

options.text: After inc(), `snapshot` (the default import) is still 0.
Writing `count = 5` in main.js sets the counter to 5 for every module.
If report.js also imports counter.js, it gets its own count, starting again at 0.

questions.explanation: Top-level await pauses the evaluation of secrets.js and of every module that depends on it, here server.js, so "server: listening" is printed only after the secrets have arrived, and server.js never sees an unfinished value. It does not block the thread: timers, I/O and modules that do not depend on secrets.js keep running, which is why metrics.js can print first. A CommonJS require() of a module graph that contains top-level await fails with ERR_REQUIRE_ASYNC_MODULE; use import() there instead.

options.text: "server: listening" is printed only after fetchSecrets() has resolved; metrics.js, which does not depend on secrets.js, may run during the wait.
The await blocks the whole Node.js process for 2 seconds: no timers, no I/O and no other module run.
server.js runs immediately and sees `secrets` as undefined until the fetch completes.
A CommonJS file can call require('./secrets.js') and receives a promise of the module.
